name: Slow Design
description:
Slow Design questions design practices centred on speed, novelty and short-term consumption. It encourages attention to duration, locality, reflection, participation, material lifecycles and the longer-term relationships people develop with designed things.

Rather than being a single procedural method, Slow Design is better understood as a set of principles through which design decisions and their consequences can be reconsidered.
whenToUse: Use Slow Design as a critical lens when a project raises questions about sustainability, longevity, consumption, repair, local context or the pace at which products and services are produced and replaced.
steps: Identify where speed, convenience or novelty shapes the current design.
Examine the product or service across a longer timeframe.
Consider material, social and environmental consequences.
Investigate opportunities for maintenance, adaptation and repair.
Consider local knowledge, production and participation.
Explore interactions that encourage reflection rather than automatic consumption.
Evaluate them according to long-term as well as immediate value.
lookOutFor: *'Slow'* does not simply mean inefficient or time-consuming.
Longer-lasting products are not automatically sustainable if their materials or systems remain harmful.
Consider who has the time and resources to participate in slower practices; slowness can carry different costs for different people.

resources.citation: Strauss, C. F. & Fuad-Luke, A. (2008). “The Slow Design Principles.”
